title: What's the difference between a violin and a fiddle? | MUSIC WORDS

entries.note: Means art of the muses, from [[from:muse]]; its Proto-Indo-European root is shared with many words relating to memory.
One of the nine mythological goddesses who presided over arts and sciences and inspired new creations; it gave [[gave:music]] and [[gave:museum]].
A close relative of [[same-root:music]], figuratively a temple to the [[from:muse]]s, who inspired creation and invention.
Originally the dancing place for the Greek chorus, then Roman seats for important people near the stage, and from the 1700s the musicians' area or the musicians.
Literally empty orchestra in Japanese; the -oke is short for a Japanese rendering of [[from:orchestra]].
Basically every string instrument is a viola; the family comes from a Latin verb meaning to exalt or be joyful, related to the Roman goddess [[see:Vitula]].
Means little [[from:viola]]; the smallest of the family, and the subject of jokes about how it differs from a [[see:fiddle]].
Short for violoncello, an odd shortening that keeps only the diminutive suffix, like calling a [[see:trumpet]] an -et.
Means a small [[from:trump]] or little horn; [[see:trombone]] means a large trumpet.
The horn that [[gave:trumpet]] its name, and also British slang for a fart.
Baroque name for similarly sized instruments, named for where the instrument is held, in contrast with the [[see:viola da gamba]].
Baroque instrument that looks like a cello because it is held in a similar position, contrasted with the [[see:viola da braccio]].
A six-string instrument invented around the same time as the [[see:violin]], and a predecessor of the [[see:double bass]].
Means big [[from:viol]]; an early version of the [[see:double bass]].
Also called a contrabass, it is bigger than a cello; its early version was the [[see:violone]].
Means quiet; it is short for [[from:pianoforte]], and as a musical marking it means quietly.
Means quiet loud, a kind of harpsichord that could also be played quietly by damping; it is itself short for [[from:gravicembalo col piano e forte]].
The full Italian name that was shortened to [[gave:pianoforte]].
Its first element comes from the Germanic word [[from:harp]], one of the few Germanic terms in the episode.
An Old English word whose root was adopted into Latin and Italian, giving [[gave:harpsichord]] and ultimately [[gave:arpeggio]].
A Germanic word whose cognates are thought to share a root with [[same-root:violin]] and [[same-root:viola]]; the hosts trade jokes about how a fiddle differs from a violin.
Probably from a Bantu word like [[from:mbanza]], one of many music words that travelled from Africa to the Americas through the slave trade.
A dance like the [[see:banjo]], brought from Africa to the Americas and then re-exported to Europe.
Hawaiian for jumping flea; Rob plays one, and the tuning chant [[see:my dog has fleas]] nods to the meaning.
A mnemonic ukulele players chant while tuning up, nodding to the jumping-flea meaning of [[see:ukulele]].
From a Persian word for three string; 12th-century sitars had three strings, but modern ones have 18 to 21, mostly sympathetic.
Probably imitates the instrument's sound and appeared in English in the early 1900s; claims that it means hollow bamboo lack evidence.
A Yolŋu Matha name for the [[equivalent:didgeridoo]], and one the hosts suggest using more widely.
Another Indigenous name for the [[equivalent:didgeridoo]] given by the hosts.
An eponym from [[from:Leon Theremin]]; it is played without touching, with two antennas sensing hand position to control pitch and volume.
Patented the device named after him, the [[see:theremin]].
Named after [[from:Adolphe Sax]], with -phone from Greek for sound; patented in 1846 as a brass clarinet, later legitimised by vaudeville, ragtime and jazz.
Belgian instrument maker with 46 patents who named his instruments after himself, including the [[see:saxophone]]; he did not live to see its heyday.
An earlier instrument [[see:Adolphe Sax]] named after himself and tried to popularise.
Another instrument [[see:Adolphe Sax]] named after himself and tried to popularise.
A later instrument [[see:Adolphe Sax]] tried to make part of the orchestra.
Probably an Italian take on French [[from:hautbois]], which then came into English; the older English name was [[see:hautboy]].
The original English word for the [[see:oboe]], an English attempt at French [[from:hautbois]], discussed in a past episode.
French for high wood, or high-pitched wood; source of [[gave:hautboy]], [[gave:hoboy]] and [[gave:oboe]].
An old English name for the [[see:oboe]], also seen as hoot boy, from French [[from:hautbois]].
A word for a tube, typical of brass names, which the hosts find straightforward.
Means a large [[from:trumpet]].
Thought to be an abbreviation of [[from:drumslade]], which is recorded earlier; similar Germanic forms appear only in compounds.
A drum beat; the name moved from the sound to the instrument and was shortened to [[gave:drum]]; the slade part is related to German [[same-root:schlagen]].
A German word meaning to hit, related to the second element of [[same-root:drumslade]].
An Old Frisian compound meaning drum beat, an example of the Germanic compounds resembling [[same-root:drumslade]].
Popular Second World War entertainer who played the banjo ukulele and sang in a comic voice, including [[see:When I'm Cleaning Windows]].
A [[see:George Formby]] song about a window cleaner spotting women in their underwear, which Rob sings.
Means wood sound, sharing its xylo- with [[same-root:xylem]]; mentioned in a previous episode, and contrasted with [[see:glockenspiel]].
Shares the xylo- element meaning wood with [[same-root:xylophone]].
German for bell play; its etymology shows how it differs from the [[see:xylophone]].
A type of xylophone with a name from Kimbundu: ma- is a plural prefix and rimba means wooden bar, an etymology similar to [[see:xylophone]].
The string stretched across a drum's lower head; it comes from an old Germanic word for a string or cord, like a trap's noose.
From the Italian for to increase; it has spread into general use, as in building to a crescendo.
Tempo marking literally meaning at ease, telling the player to play slowly and relaxed.
Tempo marking meaning fast and lively, literally cheerful.
Tempo marking meaning walking, a moderate walking pace.
Tempo marking meaning very fast.
Tempo marking meaning slow and broad.
Tempo marking meaning moderate.
Means smoothly, from the Italian for to bind, as in binding notes into a smooth surface; related to [[same-root:league]].
Related to [[same-root:legato]] through the idea of binding.
Means played in a choppy way, from the Italian for detached.
Means loudly, the counterpart of [[see:piano]]; it is the second half of [[see:pianoforte]].
Means very quietly, an intensified [[from:piano]].
Means very loudly, an intensified [[from:forte]].
Italian for middle or half; mezzo piano means fairly quietly.
Means tail, the concluding passage of a piece; indirectly related to [[same-root:coward]] via French.
Probably from a word for tail, implying an animal with its tail between its legs, plus a pejorative ending; related to [[same-root?:coda]].
Possibly shares the tail-between-the-legs idea of [[see?:coward]], though it has another theoretical origin.
Means harp-like and ultimately comes from the Germanic word [[from:harp]].
Means song added to speech, from ad- plus Latin [[from:cantus]], so speaking in an accent is singing your distinctive song.
From the same Latin song root as [[same-root:accent]].
Slang language, from the same song root as [[same-root:accent]], probably from the sing-song way such languages were spoken.
Originally meant performing every note of the scale from high to low, from medieval music theory's [[from:gamut]].
An 11th-century Benedictine monk who made music easier to memorise and read with [[see:solmization]], whose scale gave [[see:gamut]].
[[see:Guido of Arezzo]]'s system for memorising and reading music, which evolved into [[gave:solfège]].
The do-re-mi system, whose syllables come from the hymn [[from:Ut queant laxis]]; [[see:si]] was added later and renamed [[see:ti]] by [[see:Sarah Glover]].
Reportedly struggled to sing the do-re-mi song while playing guitar until someone gave her a little schnapps, then nailed it in one take.
The first syllable of Guido's scale, from the start of [[from:Ut queant laxis]]; it later became do and forms the second part of [[gave:gamut]].
A Latin hymn for St John the Baptist's day whose line-opening syllables gave the hexachord notes; the hosts translate it.
The medieval six-note series formed from syllables of [[from:Ut queant laxis]]; running the gamut means running its length.
Added later from the first letters of Sancte Iohannes in the hymn's last line, then renamed [[gave:ti]].
In the 1800s [[see:Sarah Glover]] renamed [[from:si]] as ti, which is why both names exist.
An English music teacher who renamed [[see:si]] to [[see:ti]] in the 1800s.
From [[from:gamma]], marking the note below A on Guido's scale, plus [[from:ut]]; it meant the complete range of notes in medieval music.
